title: Building a Game in C#
subtitle: Object-oriented design, re-learned from the data up
factStrip: One semester  ·  You already know how to program  ·  Homework capped at 15 minutes a night
overview: You have written objects before, in at least two languages, so this course starts past the definition.  What it shows you instead is that most of what you believe about objects is a **decision** somebody made, in the language you happened to learn first, and that other languages decided differently.

C# has been moving for a decade toward a particular set of those decisions:  data that is fixed once built, types that arrive valid or get refused, and behavior that lives beside the data.  That is where we are going, and it will look strange for a week or two.

You build the tools.  Everything the final game runs on -- dice, cards, collections, entities, a world, a command loop -- you write yourself, in order, each one arriving because the lesson before it made you feel the absence.  Every piece of it is yours, down to the bottom.
Around the middle of the semester you choose what you are actually building.  Everything after that point is scaffolding for **your** choice.
goals: Decide, member by member, what about a type can change and who is allowed to change it -- and make the compiler enforce it
Build types that are impossible to construct in an invalid state
Decide whether a behavior belongs *on* a type or *beside* it, using a test you can apply to code you are seeing for the first time
Write collections, polymorphism, and interfaces at the moment your game needs them
Read a compiler error as information
Ship a game somebody else can pick up and play

p: A **Lesson Page** -- the new idea, the vocabulary, the starter project, and the steps.  Read it, run it, work through it.
An **Assignment** -- where you turn work in, check yourself against the four stages, and write a couple of sentences about the calls you made.
**Dice** is the worked example.  We build it together, in class, on the projector, and everybody walks out with it.

**Cards** is yours.  The same idea arrives a second time as a problem you solve alone.  It is where you find out whether the lesson actually landed -- and it is the one file in this course that belongs entirely to you.
Open the folder, run it, and something happens before you have changed a line.  That is a promise I keep on purpose.
Usually the code already works.  Your job is to make it **honest** -- to find the thing that runs perfectly and is still wrong, and say why.

howItWorks.h: Homework is capped, and the cap is real
p: Fifteen minutes a night, or thirty every other meeting.  Treat that as a ceiling.
Homework consolidates syntax you have already met, and every lesson opens fresh.  Skip it entirely and you still walk in able to participate.  Class time is where the building happens.
Every lesson page and assignment has a button that opens an AI helper for that lesson.  It asks you questions and pushes you toward the answer, and it leaves the answer for you to reach.
Also:  ask the person next to you, and ask me.  Both are allowed and both work better than staring.

stagesIntro: Every assignment uses the same four stages.  They are a **map** -- where you are and what to try next.  **Made It Mine** is the target for everyone, every lesson.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: The build is red, or the change is still ahead of you.  Every lesson names the likeliest cause and the exact next thing to try.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: The thing the lesson was about is done, and the program runs.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and you did the same thing to **your** code, on your own, and can defend the calls you made.  **This is the goal for everyone.**

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and you took it somewhere the lesson left open.  The list here stays open on purpose -- that is the entire point of it.

stagesOutro: You can revise and resubmit anything.  Everything here is open to a second pass, and finding out you were wrong is most of the work.

_submitHint: Appears under 'What to turn in'.  Set to "" to omit the line entirely.
submitHint: **Getting your URL from GitHub Desktop:**  type a short summary, click **Commit to main**, then click **Push origin** at the top.  Both steps matter -- a commit that has yet to be pushed stays on your laptop, and the page I open would show your work from last week.  Then **Repository > View on GitHub** and copy the address out of your browser.  The `bin/` and `obj/` folders stay out of the repository on their own, so leave them alone.  If pushing refuses to work, zip the project folder instead and tell me what it said.
